notes.meaning: Israel had no earthly king during this era, which led to disorder across the tribes. The tribe of Dan had not yet secured its full territory because they failed to drive out the Canaanites in their assigned home. Instead of trusting God to take their allotted land, they began looking for an easier place to claim.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars note that Deborah's song in Judges 5 implies Dan had already settled its northern territory early in the period, showing that these events happened near the beginning of the judges' era.

notes.meaning: The Danites chose five capable warriors from their towns of Zorah and Eshtaol to explore the land. On their way north, these scouts stopped for the night in the hill country of Ephraim near Micah's home.

While resting near Micah's house, the scouts recognized the voice or southern accent of the young Levite. They walked over and asked him who brought him to this region and what work he was doing so far from home.
The Levite explained how Micah had made an agreement with him. Micah gave him food, clothing, and wages to serve as a personal priest for his private household shrine.

Rather than rebuking the young man for serving at an unlawful private shrine, the scouts asked him to consult God for them. They wanted to know if their scouting expedition would succeed, showing how casual they had become about God's laws.

The priest gave them a comforting answer, telling them to go in peace because the Lord was looking favorably on their journey. He offered this pleasing blessing to flatter them, though God had never sent him.

The five scouts traveled north and reached the town of Laish. They found a peaceful, trusting people who lived like the wealthy Phoenician port city of Sidon, but Laish was completely isolated and had no allies nearby to come to its rescue.
The scouts returned south to Zorah and Eshtaol to report their findings. Their fellow Danites eagerly asked what kind of land they had discovered.
The spies urged their brothers to attack immediately, describing the land as rich and fruitful. They rebuked their brothers for hesitating when such an easy prize was right before them.
The scouts explained that the people of Laish suspected no danger and had plenty of fertile land. They claimed God had given the valley to them, misusing holy language to support a self-serving raid.
A group of six hundred Danite men armed for battle marched out from Zorah and Eshtaol. This was not a quick raiding party, but an entire settlement migrating north to take a new home.
The migrating Danites set up camp just west of Kiriath-jearim in the territory of Judah. The place was called Mahaneh-dan, which means the camp of Dan, to mark the site where their army rested.
From Judah, the group marched north into the hill country of Ephraim. They traveled until they arrived outside the settlement where Micah lived.

The five scouts told the armed men that one of the houses held an ephod, household gods, and silver idols. They urged the soldiers to consider what they ought to do, hinting that they should take these religious items for themselves.
The five scouts turned off the main road and went directly to the young Levite's quarters at Micah's house. They greeted him warmly to keep him calm and friendly.
While the scouts went up to the house, the six hundred armed Danite warriors stood at the entrance gate. Their presence sent a clear threat of force to anyone who might try to stop them.

The five scouts slipped inside the shrine and took the carved image, the priest's vestment, the household gods, and the metal idol. Outside, the priest stood by the gate with the six hundred armed soldiers, distracted while the theft took place.
When the priest saw the scouts carrying Micah's sacred objects out of the shrine, he called out and asked what they were doing. He was shocked to see his chapel being looted before his eyes.

The Danites told the priest to be quiet and put his hand over his mouth. They offered him a promotion, asking whether it was better to serve as priest for one man's house or for an entire clan and tribe in Israel.
The priest was glad to receive an offer of higher status and greater influence. He took the idols and sacred vestments and joined the Danite company without showing any loyalty to Micah.
The Danites set out again, placing their children, livestock, and goods in front of the column. They put the soldiers in the rear because they expected Micah to chase after them.
After the Danites had marched down the road, Micah discovered the theft and sounded the alarm. The men living near Micah's house rallied together and caught up with the Danite rear guard.
Micah's group shouted after them, causing the Danites to turn around and face them. The soldiers mockingly asked Micah why he had gathered an armed crowd to follow them.

Micah cried out that they had stolen the gods he made and taken his priest, leaving him with nothing. His sorrow exposes the emptiness of worshiping manufactured idols that cannot even protect themselves.
The Danites warned Micah to lower his voice and stop complaining. They threatened that angry soldiers would turn on him and slaughter both him and his family if he said another word.
The Danites kept marching, and Micah turned back toward home because he saw they were far too strong for him. Might took the place of justice in a land without a godly ruler.
Taking Micah's stolen idols and his priest, the Danites arrived at the peaceful, unsuspecting town of Laish. They struck the residents with their swords and burned the city to the ground.
No nearby ally could rescue Laish, because the town sat far from Sidon in a northern valley near Beth-rehob. After destroying the inhabitants, the Danites rebuilt the city and made it their new home.
The settlers renamed the conquered town Dan in honor of their tribal ancestor, replacing its old name of Laish. The city later became famous as the northern boundary mark of Israel's territory.

The Danites set up the carved image for their own official tribal worship in the new city. Jonathan, who was a descendant of Moses through Gershom, served along with his sons as priests for Dan until the land went into captivity.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic scholarship notes that the Latin Vulgate and original Hebrew text read 'son of Moses,' and that later scribes suspended a letter to read 'Manasseh' to shield Moses' family name from the shame of idolatry.

notes.meaning: Micah's carved image stayed set up in Dan throughout the centuries while the true tabernacle of God remained at Shiloh. What started as one family's private sin grew into long-lasting national idolatry.
